summary: The last week begins. Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a borrowed colt while crowds shout Hosanna and spread cloaks on the road — then walks into the temple, looks around at everything, and leaves because it is late. The next morning he curses a fig tree that has no fruit, goes into the temple and shuts down the trading, and on the following morning the disciples find the tree dead. The authorities demand to know who authorized any of this, and he answers with a question they refuse to touch.
whyItMatters: Everything after this happens inside one week. The entry looks like a coronation and the temple action looks like a riot, and Mark wraps the second inside a story about a tree that produced nothing — which tells you how he wants the temple scene read.

context.author: Anonymous; early tradition names Mark, recording Peter's preaching
context.audience: Greek-speaking readers outside Judea, unfamiliar with temple layout and Passover crowds
context.date: Somewhere in the AD 50s–70s. If written after AD 70, the readers already knew the temple was gone
context.setting: Jerusalem at Passover, when the population swelled several times over and Rome moved extra troops in — the most volatile week of the year
context.literaryForm: Narrative with Mark's sandwich technique: the fig tree is split open and the temple action is placed inside it

outline.heading: Riding in
outline.note: A colt no one has ridden, cloaks on the road, Hosanna — and then he inspects the temple and goes to bed

outline.heading: The fig tree — outer half
outline.note: Leaves but no fruit, and it was not the season for figs

outline.heading: The temple — inner half
outline.note: Tables overturned, traffic stopped, two prophets quoted; the authorities start looking for a way to kill him

outline.heading: The tree, next morning
outline.note: Withered from the roots; teaching on faith, prayer, and forgiveness

outline.heading: By what authority?
outline.note: A question about John that traps them into saying they don't know

keyVerses.text: Jesus entered into the temple in Jerusalem. When he had looked around at everything, it being now evening, he went out to Bethany with the twelve.
keyVerses.why: The anticlimax that gives the week its tone. He inspects, says nothing, and comes back the next day.

keyVerses.text: Isn’t it written, ‘My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations’? But you have made it a den of robbers!
keyVerses.why: Two quotations doing the work — Isaiah 56 on who the temple was for, Jeremiah 7 on a building used as cover.

keyVerses.text: The chief priests and the scribes heard it, and sought how they might destroy him.
keyVerses.why: The plot moves from Galilean opposition to the temple leadership. From here it is a matter of finding the opportunity.

keyVerses.text: Whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone
keyVerses.why: Placed immediately after teaching about mountains being moved — the condition attached to the promise.

questions.question: Why ride a donkey? It seems an odd choice for a triumphal entry.
questions.answer: That is the point. Zechariah 9:9 describes a king coming to Jerusalem humble and riding on a colt, and the same passage has him cutting off the war horse and the battle bow. A Roman general entered a city on a warhorse. Choosing an unridden colt is a deliberate claim to kingship and a deliberate statement about what kind. Mark does not quote Zechariah — he stages it and lets readers who know the passage recognize it.

questions.question: What does 'Hosanna' mean?
questions.answer: It is Hebrew for 'save now' — originally a cry for help, which had become a shout of praise in festival use. The words the crowd shouts come from Psalm 118, one of the psalms sung at the great festivals. So the crowd is using liturgy, and what they add in verse 10 about 'the kingdom of our father David' shows what they think is happening: the restoration of a national kingdom. They are enthusiastic and they have the wrong idea, which is why the same city turns in a few days.

questions.question: Verse 11 is strange. He arrives to a huge welcome and then just... looks around and leaves?
questions.answer: It is one of Mark's most deliberate anticlimaxes, and only he tells it this way. Matthew has the temple cleared the same day. In Mark the parade ends with an inspection — he looks around at everything — and then he goes to Bethany because it is late. The delay makes what happens the next morning a considered act rather than a burst of temper. He has already seen it all.

questions.question: Why curse a fig tree for having no figs when Mark says it wasn't fig season?
questions.answer: The parenthesis is the difficulty, and Mark put it there himself, so he was not hiding it. Two things help. First, a fig tree in leaf normally carries early unripe buds that were edible, so leaves without anything at all is a tree advertising more than it has. Second, and more important, is where the story sits: split in half around the temple. The fig tree is Israel's own image for itself in the prophets (Jeremiah 8:13, Hosea 9:10, Micah 7:1), and Jesus has just inspected a temple full of activity. Leaves and no fruit is the verdict. Read as an isolated event about breakfast, it looks petty; read as Mark placed it, it is an enacted judgment.

questions.question: What was actually wrong with the money changers? Weren't they providing a service?
questions.answer: They were, and that is part of what makes the scene sharp. Pilgrims arrived with Roman coins bearing the emperor's image and needed temple currency; those travelling far could not bring animals and needed to buy them. The trade was necessary. What Jesus attacks is where and what it had become — filling the one court Gentiles were allowed into, in a house he says was meant to be a house of prayer for all nations. His Jeremiah quotation is precise: a den is not where robbers rob, it is where they retreat afterward and feel safe.

questions.question: How much of the temple did he actually shut down?
questions.answer: The temple complex was enormous — the outer courts covered something like thirty-five acres, with Roman troops garrisoned overlooking it during festivals. One man could not have stopped the whole operation, and the soldiers would have moved if he had. Verse 16 says he would not let anyone carry a container through, which suggests he blocked a thoroughfare for a period. It was a prophetic act — a public sign, done in the busiest week of the year, aimed at meaning rather than logistics. It was still enough to get him killed.

questions.question: Does verse 23 mean I can get anything I ask for?
questions.answer: Read alone it sounds like it, and that reading has caused real damage to people whose prayers were not answered. Three things keep it in shape. The mountain image was a known figure of speech for an impossibility, not a literal proposal. The immediate context is a withered tree and a confrontation with the temple establishment, so the subject is God's purposes, not personal wishes. And verse 25 attaches a condition Jesus himself supplies — forgive, if you have anything against anyone. The New Testament elsewhere shows unanswered prayer plainly, including in Gethsemane two chapters later, where Jesus asks for the cup to pass and it does not.

questions.question: My Bible skips verse 26, or puts it in brackets. Why?
questions.answer: Because it is missing from the oldest and most reliable Greek manuscripts and appears to have been added later by copyists, most likely borrowed from the parallel wording in Matthew 6:15. The text hosted here includes it. This is an ordinary example of how the manuscript tradition works, and modern Bibles flag it rather than quietly choosing — the same practice that puts a note at the end of Mark 16.

questions.question: Why does Jesus answer a question with a question instead of just replying?
questions.answer: It is a recognized style of rabbinic debate, not evasion. And his counter-question is exact: John's baptism, from heaven or from men? They cannot say 'from heaven' without explaining why they rejected him, and they cannot say 'from men' with a crowd standing there who considered John a prophet. Mark lets you watch them work it out in verses 31-32, which is unusually candid reporting of a private calculation. Their answer is that they do not know, which is not true, and he declines to trade on it.

questions.question: Why does the temple leadership treat this as a killing offence?
questions.answer: Because of what he interfered with and when. The temple was the religious centre, the economic engine of the city, and the basis of the chief priests' authority, which Rome tolerated so long as they kept order. Disrupting it during Passover — the festival that commemorated liberation from an empire, in a city packed with pilgrims and watched by troops — was the most dangerous act available. Verse 18 also names their other motive: they feared him, because the crowd was astonished at his teaching.

glossary.def: Hebrew for 'save now.' A cry for rescue that had become a festival shout of praise, drawn from Psalm 118.
The ridge east of Jerusalem, overlooking the temple. Zechariah 14 places God's decisive intervention there, which gives the approach route its weight.
Traders who exchanged Roman coinage, which bore the emperor's image, for currency acceptable as a temple offering. A necessary service; the dispute is over what it had displaced.
From Jeremiah 7:11, part of a sermon delivered at the temple gate warning that the building would not protect a corrupt people. A den is the hideout, not the crime scene.
The temple aristocracy, headed by the high priest. They held religious authority and, under Roman oversight, considerable civil power — and the most to lose from disorder at Passover.
